article.title: How billionaires rigged the midterms (it wasn’t just Elon)
article.author: Amanda Yee
article.content: The 2026 midterms shattered records as the most expensive election in U.S. history, with an unprecedented $12 billion that flooded campaigns nationwide. BreakThrough News journalist Amanda Yee discusses how behind the massive price tag lay a coordinated ruling-class offensive: billionaire oligarchs and special interest PACs, from AIPAC targeting pro-Palestine progressives to Big Tech and crypto power brokers, bought bipartisan influence to deregulate industry, crush dissent, and protect corporate wealth. Yee explains who wrote the checks and reveals how America’s electoral system was engineered to serve capital over the working class. #breakthroughnews ****** Rough transcript follows: $12 billion—that’s how much was spent on the 2026 midterms, marking them as the most expensive elections in U.S. history. Here are the top contributors to this midterm cycle, according to OpenSecrets. If you look at the bar graph, it’s essentially a who’s who of billionaires. Elon Musk is at the top, followed by Zionist casino magnate Miriam Adelson and Michael Bloomberg. A bunch of tech oligarchs, including the LinkedIn co-founder and the CEO of Blackstone, are also on the list. Republicans have outraised and outspent Democrats across the board this cycle. However, the real story isn’t the party split; it’s who’s writing the checks and what they’re buying. Three special interest groups have dominated this cycle, spending historic amounts to shape Congress in their favor: AIPAC, big tech, and crypto. Let’s start with AIPAC. AIPAC contributed nearly $25 million to candidates and political committees in 2026 through September 30th. After September 30th, support for Israel became a massive political liability due to the ongoing situation in Gaza. More candidates are facing scrutiny for taking AIPAC money. In October, AIPAC announced they would no longer issue endorsements or make direct contributions to candidates. However, this doesn’t mean they’re stopping their spending; they’re just changing how they spend. This is where the United Democracy Project (UDP), AIPAC’s affiliated super PAC, comes in. UDP acts as a cover for AIPAC money. You might remember them from 2024 when they spent over $9 million to unseat Jamal Bowman and another $9 million to defeat Cori Bush. Both candidates were critical of Israel and lost their races after UDP’s involvement. AIPAC’s biggest investment in the primaries was a flop. In the Michigan Democratic primary, AIPAC and UDP spent $30 million trying to protect Haley Stevens’s seat, but she lost to Abdel Sayed. UDP then spent $9 million in the general election to support Republican Mike Rogers. AIPAC funds Democrats too, especially when they’re running against progressives. For example, in California’s 14th congressional district, AIPAC is backing Melissa Hernandez against progressive Democrat Aisha Wahab. Wahab, who has called the situation in Gaza a genocide, won a special election to finish Eric Swalwell’s term. UDP spent $1.6 million across both races to block Wahab, including $800,000 on attack ads. Individual billionaire donors also shape Israeli policy. Robert Kraft, a major donor to UDP and AIPAC, and Miriam Adelson, who donated over $66 million this cycle, are significant contributors. Hedge fund billionaire Paul Singer gave $49 million to Republican-aligned PACs and $2.6 million to UDP. Now, let’s talk about big tech. Elon Musk took the top spot for highest donor, contributing $446 million to Republican candidates and PACs. Over $200 million went to Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton’s Senate campaign. Musk also donated $5 million to Texas Governor Greg Abbott’s reelection bid. Other notable tech donors include Benjamin Horowitz and Mark Andreessen, who spent over $55 million and $43 million, respectively. OpenAI co-founder Greg Brockman and his wife Anna contributed $50 million to Republican causes. These donors launched the “Leading the Future” PAC to fund candidates committed to blocking AI regulation and cutting China out of the AI race. Finally, let’s discuss crypto. The Winklevoss twins, co-founders of Gemini Crypto Exchange, contributed nearly $24 million, mostly to MAGA Inc. Chris Larsen, founder of Ripple Labs, donated at least $22.5 million, with $12 million opposing California’s proposed billionaire wealth tax. Larsen also supports the “Invest in Tomorrow Coalition” PAC, which targets Republicans and DSA members who oppose renewable energy incentives. Fairshake, crypto’s own PAC, spent $95 million this cycle, backing 33 House incumbents. They’ve disclosed at least $1 million in donations to campaigns of key committee members like Brian Steil, French Hill, and Bill Huizenga. Fairshake also contributed to Democrats like Janelle Bynum, Derek Tran, and Steven Horsford. House Ways and Means Committee Chair Jason Smith, who has tried to subpoena Breakthrough over funding, is also backed by Fairshake. In conclusion, whether it’s foreign policy, AI regulation, or crypto protectionism, $12 billion bought significant access this election. This cycle encapsulates the rule of billionaires in the U.S., where choices are influenced by AIPAC, big tech, or crypto.
